Infill Pattern Guide

Instaread

 3D printing infill patterns control how strong, light, and fast your model turns out.  In OrcaSlicer, you’ll find around 15-20 infill patterns. Pick a dense but inefficient pattern, and you waste  filament. Pick one that’s too sparse, and your model bends or cracks under pressure.  

Urban & Regional Planning

Many users test fill pattern strength by running their own  print experiments, but we’ve already compared the main options to give you a clear starting point. For example, Gyroid offers balanced strength in all directions, Triangles deliver maximum rigidity, and Lightning minimizes material use for faster prints.

This 3D printing infill patterns guide shows how internal geometries impact print strength, time, and filament usage. While we’ll use OrcaSlicer to demonstrate, these properties apply across all slicers. Learn how to select the best infill pattern to save filament and improve print success.

 Infill Pattern Fundamentals

Infill is the internal structure, and the infill patterns determine how material is distributed inside a 3D print. Instead of printing models fully solid, infill patterns provide internal support while saving filament. In OrcaSlicer, it appears as a mesh or lattice (usually shown in red) when you preview your model. Main types of infill:

  • Sparse infill: Found inside the model. You can change its shape and density to balance weight and strength. 
  • Solid infill: Seen on the top and bottom layers or dense sections. It’s fully solid (100%) and improves surface strength and finish, but consumes more filament and time.

Each pattern, Grid, Triangles, Honeycomb, or Gyroid, offers a tradeoff between strength, speed, and material efficiency. The right pattern depends on what your print needs most: strength, speed, or flexibility.

Graphic Design

What Is Infill Density?

Infill density shows how solid the model’s interior is, measured in percentage, where 0% is hollow, and 100% is completely solid. Adjusting the infill density percentage changes the part’s weight, strength, and printing time. Here’s how it affects prints:

  • Higher density (40-60%) means stronger, heavier, and longer prints. Best for mechanical or load-bearing parts.
  • Medium density (20-30%) means balanced durability and efficiency. Ideal for everyday prints.
  • Low density (1-10%) is best for lightweight, fast prints suited for decorative or display models.

Tips!

In OrcaSlicer infill settings, you can preview how density and pattern interact. Understanding 3D printer infill density helps get strong and visually clean prints. Here are some tips we got from our tests: 

  • Preview your model in the slicer to see how density changes the inner layout.
  • For functional parts, increase density gradually rather than jumping to 100%.
  • For cosmetic prints, reducing sparse infill to 2-5% saves material and time but may affect surface quality.
  • Use adaptive infill patterns (like Support Cubic or Lightning) for prints that need top-layer support without extra material. (More on each pattern later)

Key Performance Factors for Choosing the Right Infill Pattern

Choosing the right infill pattern comes down to how infill geometry shapes real print behavior. While you can preview it through infill simulation in Orca slicing software, the actual outcome depends on factors like strength, print time, and layer consistency.

3D Printers & Scanners

Strength

Strength refers to a part’s ability to resist forces, both horizontally (X-Y) and vertically (Z-direction). Some patterns excel in X-Y strength yet poorly in Z-direction strength, meaning they’re strong across the print bed but weak between layers. 

An isotropic infill structure (such as a gyroid or cubic) maintains similar strength in all axes, while an anisotropic infill structure favours one direction. In our tests, patterns with balanced strength across axes perform better for multi-directional loads.

Material Usage & Print Time

Efficient use of filament and shorter print cycles are key for many projects. Infill patterns vary widely in infill efficiency and print speed optimization because of how they direct the nozzle movement and generate internal paths.

A good slicing strategy ensures print head movement efficiency and consistent material flow, meaning fewer wasted moves or over-extrusion. We found that patterns like the support cubic pattern reduce material use while still offering usable strength.

Layer Time Variability

Layer time variability means how much print time changes from one layer to the next. Patterns like grid or rectilinear  print layers evenly, giving smooth surfaces and stable cooling. Complex infills such as gyroid or honeycomb take longer on some layers, which can cause uneven cooling and minor surface differences in  3D print quality.

Mathematics

Lower layer time variability improves surface finish and reduces print failures in advanced slicing workflows.

Pattern Categories & Deep Dive: Properties, Strength, & Speed

OrcaSlicer provides around 15-20 3D print infill types, each designed for different applications. We tested these patterns to give you a general overview, not exact model-specific data. You can preview time, infill material usage, and 3D print layer time variability directly in OrcaSlicer before  printing.

This infill pattern strength test doesn’t count in material type; it’s a general guide to help you pick the right pattern for your needs. We summarized data from our tests and major studies to provide an unbiased look at the real-world overall performance of infill patterns.

Fast & Simple Patterns (For Speed Priority)

These patterns prioritize printing speed and simplicity. Perfect for prototypes, drafts, and parts where structural strength isn’t critical.

Monotonic & Monotonic Line

  • Best for: Top surfaces, aesthetic prints
  • Strength: Normal/Normal
  • Speed: Average  print speed 
  • When to use: Visible top layers, smooth finishes

These patterns appear in a single, continuous direction without overlapping the perimeter.

Graphic Design

  • Monotonic creates uniform top surfaces on flat layers, ideal when you want a clean finish without perimeter overlap
  • Monotonic Line avoids overlap entirely, making it better for complex geometry or reducing stringing issues

Both work excellently for top solid infill, especially on models with large flat areas. Pair them with ironing for even cleaner results. They handle internal solid infill and extra solid infill layers where you need strategic reinforcement. They do not use that much material and take a moderate time to print. 

Rectilinear & Aligned Rectilinear

  • Best for: Basic prints, prototypes
  • Strength: Normal-Low (XY), Low (Z)
  • Speed: Average print speed 

Rectilinear prints parallel lines in one direction per layer, rotating 90° for the next layer. This creates low vertical bonding since layers don’t interconnect well. Aligned Rectilinear prints all layers in the same direction, with no rotation. This creates excellent perpendicular strength but terrible parallel strength. It’s faster than standard rectilinear but structurally weaker. Best for rapid prototyping where loads come from predictable directions.

Our tests showed that rectilinear performed poorly in both tensile and compression compared to  3D patterns. Z-direction strength was 60% higher than XY, typical for 2D patterns. Overall, we found rectilinear faster and more material-efficient because it prints in one direction per layer. 

3D Printers & Scanners

  • Insight

Grid prints both directions on each layer, creating stronger support for top surfaces but increasing time and material at crossings. Use a grid for strength, rectilinear for speed. Or you can use the Zig Zag infill pattern for improved results.

 Zig Zag & Cross Zag

  • Best for: General-purpose printing
    Strength: Normal-Low to Normal
  • Speed: Average print speed 

Zig Zag prints continuous straight lines in alternating directions within each layer, forming a zigzag pattern. The nozzle extrudes continuously with minimal retractions, increasing speed.

Adjust the infill rotation step to change how the pattern looks between layers. We found that Zig Zag supports symmetric infill along the Y-axis, perfect for models with two identical halves that need matching internal structure.

A similar type is Cross Zag. It builds on Zig Zag by introducing directional control at line intersections using the infill shift step parameter. This creates a rectilinear-like crosshatch with adjustable orientation. When the shift step is set to 0, it behaves like a standard rectilinear.

Urban & Regional Planning

  • Use these patterns when you need balanced speed and moderate strength, like prototypes and non-functional models. They’re faster than complex patterns like grid or cubic because the print head follows an uninterrupted path.

Line Pattern

  • Best for: Quick prints, drafts
  • Strength: Low (XY and Z)
  • Speed: Fastest basic pattern

The line pattern resembles rectilinear, but the lines don’t overlap within a layer. Each layer prints in one direction, and the next layer flips in the opposite direction. The extruded lines rotate at an acute angle rather than staying parallel.

This is one of the fastest infill patterns available. The non-overlapping lines eliminate crossings, reducing print head movement and material buildup.

Tests showed mid-range compression strength, better than grid and rectilinear, but weaker than 3D patterns. In Z-direction compression, the strength was surprisingly strong. XY compression showed moderate performance.

The structural integrity of the model seemed limited, so we don’t recommend this infill for load-bearing applications.

Visual Art & Design

High-Strength Patterns (For Structural Parts)

When your print needs to withstand real forces, these are your patterns. They excel in compression and tensile tests, making them ideal for mechanical components and load-bearing applications. Choose these when strength outweighs speed concerns. They’re the best infill patterns for compressive strength in most scenarios.

Grid Pattern

  • Best for: Load-bearing parts, mechanical components
  • Strength: High (XY and Z)
  • Speed: Fast

Grid creates a mesh by  printing two sets of lines that cross perpendicularly in each layer. This best infill pattern for tensile strength, creating overlapping intersections that provide substantial structural support. Grid follows a two-layer perpendicular structure, but unlike rectilinear (which alternates direction between layers), it prints both directions on every single layer. This creates a true crosshatch mesh with reinforced junctions.

Our testing revealed mixed results. In tensile and compression tests, the grid ranked low. However, Z-direction strength was 70% higher than XY, typical for 2D patterns where layers stack directly. Still, it’s stronger than rectilinear and better for supporting top surfaces.

Mathematics

  • Insight

While testing, we heard most of the noise while printing the grid pattern. The crossing points accumulate material, so be ready to hear clicking or scraping as the nozzle moves over them, especially at higher speeds.

Triangles & Tri-hexagon

  • Best for: Horizontal stress applications, brackets, mounts, best infill pattern for PETG applications
  • Strength: High (XY), Normal to Normal-High (Z)
  • Speed: Average 

Triangles create a geometric grid where lines cross at 60° angles instead of 90°. Even before testing, our models of triangles are most durable. Visually, at the triangle vertices, three lines meet simultaneously.

This creates significant material buildup that can cause nozzle drag and noise, similar to a grid but more pronounced. Tri-hexagon solves this by offsetting the pattern to prevent triple overlaps. It combines triangular and hexagonal shapes. Use it to get excellent XY strength and improved Z-direction performance to reduce printing issues.

CAD & CAM

For compression, triangles consistently outperformed grid and rectilinear in all conditions. Z-direction compression was strongest, reinforcing the 2D pattern behavior.

Cubic Family (Cubic, Quarter Cubic, Adaptive Cubic)

  • Best for: All-directional strength needs, functional parts
  • Strength: High (all directions)
  • Speed: Less than average 

Cubic patterns (Cubic, Quarter Cubic, Adaptive Cubic) create diagonally-stacked cubes. This infill pattern provides true  3D, isotropic strength (force distributes equally across X, Y, Z directions).

Unlike 2D patterns showing 60% XY weakness, our tests confirmed Cubic’s minimal directional preference and top compression performance. Quarter Cubic improved XY strength further. Adaptive Cubic intelligently varies density, denser near walls, sparser internally, saving 25-30% material/time on large prints while maintaining strength.

Ideal for unpredictable multi-directional forces. The only trade-off is that it takes 125% longer  print time than average, but superior to tri-hexagon in multi-directional loading.

Graphic Design

  • Insight

In OrcaSlicer, Support Cubic is a specialized low-density version designed specifically for support layers before top shells (not for structural infill). It uses far less material than Lightning but provides better strength.

Honeycomb Patterns (2D, 3D, Lateral) 

  • Best for: Maximum strength, aerospace applications
  • Strength: High (2D), Normal-High (3D variants)
  • Material Usage: High (2D), Normal-Low (3D)

2D Honeycomb uses hexagonal cells with double-width walls, preventing path tearing. Our tests ranked it best/second-best for tensile and compression, 60% stronger Z-direction than XY. 3D Honeycomb prints squares/octagons vertically for multi-directional strength with better material efficiency than 2D, though still slow. Vertical Honeycomb rotates the pattern upward for low-density structures like airplane wings.

This type of lateral honeycomb pattern provides good torsional stiffness at lower densities than standard honeycomb. In OrcaSlicer infill settings, you can adjust the overhang angle to prevent layers from separating.

Urban & Regional Planning

  • Insight

The print time doubles versus rectilinear due to constant direction changes. Another is that it uses 25% more material. For most prints, the cubic or gyroid offers better speed-to-strength balance without using too much material.

Advanced Mathematical Patterns (For Premium Performance)

These patterns use complex mathematical principles to achieve optimal strength-to-weight ratios. They’re computationally intensive to slice and slower to print, but deliver exceptional performance for high-end functional parts.

Gyroid – The Gold Standard

  • Best for: High-end functional parts, flexible prints
  • Strength: High (isotropic-equal in all directions)
  • Speed: Ultra-High print time

Gyroid infill uses sine-wave curves in a 3D structure, offering uniform strength in all directions. Our tests showed consistent mid-to-high performance regardless of force direction. Its interconnected design allows resin filling for hybrid structures.

Visual Art & Design

The complex curves do increase slicing time, especially with intricate models. Despite this, gyroid provides premium strength without excessive material use, and it’s stronger than most 2D patterns (even faster than honeycomb).

It’s ideal for parts facing multi-directional stress and works excellently with flexible  filaments like TPU/TPE due to its curved, non-intersecting paths. 

TPMS Family (TPMS-D, TPMS-FK)

  • Best for: Energy absorption, isotropic strength
  • Strength: High to Normal-High (isotropic)
  • Speed: High to Ultra-High

TPMS patterns are mathematically defined surfaces that repeat in 3D with minimal surface area. They look like efficient natural structures, like soap bubbles. TPMS-D (Schwarz Diamond) combines rigid linear elements with smooth transitions, offering gyroid-like uniform strength but faster slicing (use it when gyroid is too slow). TPMS-FK (Fischer-Koch S) mimics bone microstructure with complex curves for superior load distribution and shock absorption.

Our tests showed TPMS-D balances performance for complex models, while TPMS-FK excels at impact resistance and energy absorption. These are perfect for protective cases, grips, or shock mounts. Both provide high strength with normal material usage.

Cross Hatch

  • Best for: General purpose with good strength
  • Strength: Normal-High (XY and Z)
  • Speed: High print time

Cross Hatch bridges linear patterns (fast, weaker) and curved patterns (slow, stronger), using linear paths instead of curves for easier slicing. It’s stronger than basic grid but weaker than full 3D patterns. It was quieter than the gyroid due to fewer intersections and reduced vibration.

Mathematics

However, internal corners create stress concentration points; our tests showed gyroid’s curves distribute stress better. Cross-hatch works well for everyday parts needing balanced speed, reasonable strength, and quiet operation with tighter fill than a simple grid. Go for 3D patterns like Cubic, Gyroid, or TPMS-D for maximum uniform strength, flexible filaments, or high-compression applications.

Specialty & Lightweight Patterns

These patterns are for ultra-fast prototyping, flexible materials, or minimal material consumption. They sacrifice structural strength for other benefits.

Lightning Infill

  • Best for: Non-structural parts, display models, rapid prototyping
  • Strength: Low (XY and Z)
  • Speed: Ultra-Low (fastest pattern available)

Lightning creates a sparse, tree-like branching structure that densifies toward top surfaces, providing minimal support for top layers without filling interiors. It’s the speed champion with dramatically reduced  print times and up to 80% material savings, ideal for large display models, decorative pieces, or quick prototypes.

Graphic Design

Our tests showed it provides adequate top-layer support for non-functional parts while using ultra-low material.

However, it’s strictly for mockups, visual prototypes, and decorative objects, never for durable models. For durability and speed, it’s better to pick support Cubic. Choose Lightning for the absolute minimum material and fastest  printing times.

Concentric

  • Best for: 100% infill, flexible materials, curved geometry
  • Strength: Low (XY),  Normal (Z)
  • Speed: Normal-Low

Concentric creates progressively smaller rings following your model’s outer contour, circles for cylinders, nested squares for squares. It’s perfect for vase mode and the best choice for flexible filaments like TPU/TPE. A concentric infill pattern allows natural flex without weak points between perpendicular lines.

Our tests showed concentric ranks first for Z-direction tensile strength and second for Z-direction compression using official ASTM standards. But that showed that XY compression would be weaker. It creates beautiful visual effects with transparent filaments as light passes through parallel loops. Normal material usage, normal-low print time, with zero layer variability, make it an underdog contender worth considering.

Locked Zag

  • Best for: Custom strength distribution
  • Strength: Normal-Low (XY and Z)
  • Speed: High print time

Locked Zag combines skeleton-and-skin systems within Zig Zag, creating two infill densities in one print. In Orcaslicer, you can independently adjust skeleton density, skin density, thickness, and interconnection (lock depth).

Urban & Regional Planning

Our tests recommend 50% lock depth for optimal bonding between systems. It uses more material than standard Zig Zag but less than full-density, perfect for targeted reinforcement near mounting holes or stress points while keeping other areas lighter.

Lateral Lattice

  • Best for: Specialized applications requiring flexibility
  • Strength: Normal-Low (XY), Low (Z)
  • Speed: Normal-Low

We didn’t test its strength as Lateral Lattice is a weak pattern made for bending, not strength. You can adjust two angles to control bending direction; each angle changes layer orientation (0° is vertical) to match where stress occurs.

It’s only useful for special projects where you want something to flex or compress in a specific way, like a custom hinge or squeeze toy. Don’t use it for normal prints because it’s too weak. It uses normal material and looks smooth on the outside.

Aesthetic & Decorative Patterns

These last patterns prioritize visual appeal over structural performance. They’re designed for artistic prints, decorative pieces, or when the infill will be visible through transparent materials. 

3D Printers & Scanners

 Hilbert Curve

  • Best for: Decorative surfaces, artistic prints
  • Strength: Low (XY), Normal (Z)
  • Speed: Extra-High print time

The Hilbert Curve is a space-filling fractal that creates a continuous, non-crossing maze-like path. Visually stunning with transparent  filaments, it produces distinctive artistic effects on top layers.

However, constant direction changes drastically increase print time, longer than honeycomb but similar material usage to rectilinear. Our tests show that it’s poor for structural parts but looks great. It creates large connected cavities suitable for post-print resin filling. 

Archimedean Chords

  • Best for: Artistic prints, resin-filling applications
  • Strength: Low (XY), Normal (Z)
  • Speed: Average print time 

Archimedean Chords creates elegant concentric spiral arcs with flowing curves. Like the Hilbert Curve, it’s visually striking with translucent filaments and resin-fillable due to interconnected cavities.

CAD & CAM

However, it’s faster and more efficient, printing between concentric and rectilinear speeds with less material than Hilbert. Similar to concentric infill, Archimedean Chords help with flexibility when printing with TPU or TPE filaments. 

Octagram Spiral

  • Best for: Decorative applications only
  • Strength: Low (XY), Normal (Z)
  • Speed: Average print time

Octagram Spiral creates eight-pointed star patterns in a spiral formation. This pattern is purely decorative and offers minimal structural strength. It produces striking visual effects when used with transparent materials or on visible top layers.

The material usage is similar to Archimedean Chords, but it prints slightly longer due to the complexity of the star points. Like other spiral patterns, it can be filled with resin thanks to its large connected compartments. Our tests confirm this pattern is only for artistic prints, not functional parts.

How to Use These Fill Patterns in OrcaSlicer (Beginner Steps)

Now that you know the specs of each infill pattern for  3D prints, open OrcaSlicer and start creating! Here’s how to change the infill pattern and the infill density in Orca Slicer: 

Mathematics

  1. Open OrcaSlicer and load your model.
  2. Go to Infill settings. Set infill density first (e.g., 20-30%).
  3. Select infill pattern from the dropdown (pick one from above).
  4. Check for advanced options (e.g., adaptive density, support infill settings). If you are new, keep those defaults off.
  5. Preview the slice and use the layer preview to inspect the internal infill geometry and how many shells/walls are around it.
  6. Start the  print, monitor the first layers. After printing, test the part (fit, strength, appearance) and iterate next time if needed.

Take Away: Choosing The Right Infill Pattern In Orca Slicer 

Choosing the best infill pattern in Orca Slicer depends on what your print needs most. For maximum durability, try Adaptive Cubic or Gyroid. Need speed? Lightning delivers fast results with minimal material. This infill pattern comparison shows that each pattern serves a specific purpose, whether it’s strength, efficiency, or aesthetics.

Start by identifying your priority, then select the appropriate pattern. Adjust infill density between 15-50% for standard prints (go high for functional parts). One last tip is that adding more walls provides better strength than simply increasing the infill percentage. The walls carry most structural load while infill supports the top layers. 

Graphic Design

FAQs

Q1. What patterns work best for top and bottom surface infill?

OrcaSlicer offers eight surface options for top and bottom surface infill. They include Monotonic, Monotonic Line, Rectilinear, Aligned Rectilinear, Concentric, Hilbert Curve, Archimedean Chords, and Octagram Spiral. 

Q2. How can I achieve smooth finishes with different infill patterns?

Add three to four wall perimeters for superior surface quality. Use 15-20% infill with Cubic or Adaptive Cubic patterns for functional parts. For decorative pieces, disable top layers and use Honeycomb with doubled sparse infill width.

Q3. What mistakes should I avoid when selecting infill patterns?

Never use 100% infill unless necessary; it wastes material without meaningful strength gains. Avoid using Gyroid for every print since it’s unnecessarily slow. Prioritize thicker walls over high infill percentages for better strength-to-material efficiency.

Visual Art & Design

Q4. Which infill pattern performs best overall?

No single pattern dominates every application. Gyroid excels for organic models requiring multi-directional strength. 3D Honeycomb suits mechanical parts with uniform loads and faster print times. Your choice depends on specific project requirements.

Q5. Do combined infill patterns increase print strength?

Yes, layering different patterns significantly boosts strength by distributing stress evenly. Combined patterns like Grid with others can improve tensile strength over 100% compared to single-pattern designs through better load distribution.

Q6. What is the fastest infill pattern available?

Lightning infill prints fastest by creating sparse branching structures supporting only top surfaces while leaving interiors hollow. 

Q7. How does infill density impact print time?

Higher density increases print time significantly as the  printer fills more internal space. For example, 80% infill takes considerably longer than 20%. Lower density speeds printing and reduces filament consumption for non-functional parts.

Urban & Regional Planning

Q8. What infill percentage suits everyday prints?

Most standard prints work well with 20-30% infill, providing adequate strength without wasting material. Display models need only 10-15%, while functional components facing routine stress benefit from 40%. Reserve 50-60% for load-bearing parts.

Q9. Can I change infill patterns mid-print?

Yes, advanced slicers like OrcaSlicer support pattern changes within single prints using modifier meshes. This strengthens critical areas while conserving material elsewhere. Assign different patterns or densities to specific sections for optimized results.

Q10. Does infill affect the final print weight?

Yes, higher infill percentages add more internal material, increasing overall weight proportionally. Lower infill creates lighter prints, beneficial for decorative models or prototypes. Lightning infill weighs significantly less than Grid at identical percentages.

Q11. Which infill pattern provides maximum strength?

Triangular and Honeycomb patterns deliver exceptional strength by distributing forces evenly. Triangular excels in XY compression, while 2D Honeycomb ranks highest in tensile and compression tests. For balanced multi-directional strength, choose Gyroid or Cubic.

3D Printers & Scanners

Q12. How do I balance speed and strength effectively?

Start with 30-50% infill and three to four wall perimeters for functional parts. Select Gyroid for strength with efficiency, or Grid for balanced everyday use. Skip unnecessary supports for overhangs above 45 degrees to save time.
